parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand dollars, abbreviated G
to lance is to cut open with a blade

explanation.surface: Someone smartened up and then had a thousand-dollar haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looked sharp' reads as dressing smartly, but here it means looked quickly, as 'look sharp' means hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: To glance is to take a quick look, and doing something sharp means doing it swiftly.

parts.note: in Genesis, Zilpah bore Jacob a son named Gad
gets means obtains

explanation.surface: A biblical figure acquires clever devices.
explanation.walkthrough: Zilpah was Leah's handmaid, and her son Gad founded one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gadgets are small clever devices or tools, ingenious mechanical contrivances.

indicators.note: contrived means artificially worked out, so the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a film is too artificial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrived' rearranges all fifteen letters of CINEMA ART AND TOO; the whole clue also describes a cartoon, contrived film art.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartoon film is a form of cinema art built from drawn frames, so wholly contrived.

parts.note: the part of the lower leg behind the shin shares its name with the young animal that veal comes from

explanation.surface: A butcher's cut from a joint of veal.
explanation.definitionFit: The fleshy back of the lower leg and the young cow both carry this name, and veal is that young cow's meat.

parts.note: a physicist's measure of how compact a body's matter is, read as how thick it is

explanation.surface: A comment on someone's bulk.
explanation.definitionFit: Density is mass per volume, how thickly packed a body's substance is; 'thickness' of a liquid means the same.

clue.text: Clean son followed by a tiny young dog

indicators.note: followed by places the next pieces after the first one

parts.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son
wee is Scottish for tiny
a pup is a young dog

explanation.surface: A boy tidies up after a little puppy.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweep up is to clean a floor by brushing dirt together.

indicators.note: on, read with board as aboard ship, puts the next piece within the ship's letters

parts.note: in crosswords being on board means on a steamship, abbreviated SS
ample means quite enough, plentiful

explanation.surface: A diner on a ship has had plenty to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' is the stock way to put a word inside SS, the steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: Samples, as a verb, are small tastes or tries of food or drink.

indicators.note: topless means losing the top, the first letter of the word beach

explanation.surface: Every nudist beach comes with a bather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' removes B from BEACH; 'has one' is filler leading to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Each and every both mean all members taken individually.

clue.text: Describes it snap badly, a weak character we hear

indicators.note: badly means the words it snap are put in a poor order and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: we hear says the words are spoken, giving a word that sounds like them

parts.note: a poor trait is a weak quality of character

explanation.surface: A bad snapshot captures someone's flawed character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' turns IT SNAP into PAINTS; 'we hear' turns POOR TRAIT into its sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To paint a portrait of something is an idiom for describing it vividly in words.

clue.text: Eve's hip dislocated makes her irritable

indicators.note: dislocated means put out of place, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Eve's put her hip out, and it has made her cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dislocated' rearranges EVESHIP; the apostrophe adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Peevish describes someone fretful and easily annoyed.

parts.note: boring here means making holes, and training recruits is drill on the parade ground

explanation.surface: A dull piece of kit used to train soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' seems to mean dull, but it means cutting holes; the question mark marks the joke of a device for parade-ground drill.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool that bores holes is a drill, and drilling is also how sergeants train recruits.

definitions.meaning: split as ex (former) plus am (morning), it means past the morning
a test or examination of knowledge

explanation.surface: A test held after lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a joke: EX means former and AM means morning, so 'ex-a.m.' is after the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: An exam is a formal test, an inspection of what a student knows; former morning is after noon.

clue.text: Let it be put in place of a name

indicators.note: be put in place means the letters are put in a new place, rearranged

explanation.surface: Let it stand in place of a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be put in place' rearranges LETIT; 'of a' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: A title is the name of a book, film or person's rank.

clue.text: Case for the sewers in the Tuileries

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the words that follow, across their boundary

explanation.surface: A storm-drain casing in a Paris garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewers' looks like drains but means people who sew; the Tuileries is a Paris garden.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles and thread.

indicators.note: strange means odd, so the letters of evils are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: Weird wickedness and masks.
explanation.definitionFit: Veils are coverings that hide the face, so they work as disguises.

indicators.note: appears before puts the bear first and the next piece after it

parts.note: Yogi Bear is the cartoon bear

indicators.note: mid- takes the middle letter of the word morning

explanation.surface: A bear shows up before mid-morning.
explanation.definitionFit: A yogin is a practitioner of yoga, often living a life of austere self-denial.

clue.text: Backdrop to the situation at railway termini

parts.note: the scene is the situation or setting of events

indicators.note: termini are the end stations, so the first and last letters of railway

explanation.surface: Background to things at the ends of the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'termini' looks like stations but takes R and Y, the first and last letters of 'railway'.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre scenery is the painted backdrop behind the actors.

clue.text: Put up with Thomas C Strange

indicators.note: strange means odd, so the letters are rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: Tolerating a man called Thomas C. Strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like a surname, but it rearranges THOMASC.
explanation.definitionFit: To stomach something is to tolerate it, as in 'I can't stomach him'.

clue.text: Finished up in the brine rather drunk

definitions.meaning: food preserved in salt water or vinegar

explanation.surface: A drinker who has ended up in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Onions kept in brine are preserved that way, and the slang word for tipsy is the same.

parts.note: a peri is a fairy in Persian folklore
to wig is an old verb meaning to scold or rebuke

explanation.surface: A Persian fairy is superb at telling people off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' seems to mean excellent but means a head covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A periwig is a powdered wig worn on top of the head.

indicators.note: turned means the word had is read backwards

parts.note: Lias is a layer of blue limestone rock found in southern England

explanation.surface: Something had turned to stone among the blooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses HAD into DAH; Lias is a geological term crosswords use for rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahlias are bright garden blooms from Mexico.

clue.text: Not quite all there? That's rather unfair

definitions.meaning: slightly mad or not fully complete
somewhat unjust or out of order

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a person is mad, then calls the remark unkind.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means slightly odd in the head, and also somewhat unjust or out of order.

clue.text: French ruffians cause pain in uppish health resort

indicators.note: in means the second piece goes inside the first
uppish in a down clue means reading upwards, so the word spa runs backwards

parts.note: a spa is a health resort with mineral springs
an ache is a pain

explanation.surface: Thugs from France cause suffering at a snooty spa.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'uppish' means read upwards, so the resort is reversed; 'in' puts the pain inside it. Apaches were Paris street thugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Apaches were Parisian street gangsters of the early 1900s, named after the American people.

clue.text: Soames Forsyte's daughter hugs an idle fellow

indicators.note: hugs means the outer piece wraps around the inner one

parts.note: Fleur is Soames's daughter in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga

explanation.surface: A novelist's heroine embraces a lazy man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Forsyte Saga is John Galsworthy's series of novels about an English family.
explanation.definitionFit: A flaneur is a man who strolls about idly, watching city life.

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, a British army corps
RE is the Royal Engineers, another British army corps

explanation.surface: Soldiers of an uncommon kind.
explanation.walkthrough: One phrase supplies two British army units, the Royal Artillery and the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare means seldom found, uncommon.

clue.text: Hal accidentally caught by a European mounted lancer

indicators.note: caught by means held inside the other piece

parts.note: un is French for a, the European's word

indicators.note: accidentally means by chance, so the letters of Hal are jumbled

explanation.surface: Hal is accidentally captured by a European horseman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a European' looks like a person, but it is the French article UN; 'accidentally' turns HAL into HLA.
explanation.definitionFit: An uhlan was a cavalryman armed with a lance in Polish and German armies.

indicators.note: a little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Get on a small, calm horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' seems a verb for getting on a horse, but it names a volcano.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is a volcano in Sicily, and Mount is part of its name.

parts.note: in Robert Louis Stevenson's tale, the doctor's evil alter ego is the worse of his two selves

explanation.surface: A remark about an author's spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better half' suggests a wife; in Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde the evil self is the worse half.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Hyde is the wicked other self of Dr Jekyll in the Stevenson novella.

clue.text: Like a man who won at Wimbledon

definitions.text: Like a man who won at Wimbledon

parts.note: as means like
he is a man, the male pronoun

explanation.surface: Resembling a Wimbledon champion.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ashe, the American player, won the Wimbledon men's singles title in 1975.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was the tennis player who beat Jimmy Connors in the 1975 Wimbledon final.

clue.text: Who, in the dog days, can become bitter-sweet?

indicators.note: can become means the letters of the phrase change into something else

explanation.surface: Asks who, in high summer, turns sour and sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can become' rearranges all fifteen letters of WHO IN THE DOG DAYS; bitter-sweet is another name for this plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant Solanum dulcamara is called bittersweet because its berries taste first bitter then sweet.

parts.note: looks is slang for glances, and the males of the flock are meant too

explanation.surface: Someone tends the farm's geese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks after' seems to mean tends, but 'looks' is the noun, as in 'take a gander', and male geese come after the flock.
explanation.definitionFit: A gander is a male goose, and in slang a gander is a look.

clue.text: Casual wear for a Devonshire diner

definitions.meaning: a knitted jumper for informal dress
a jokey reading as someone who eats sweets, said in a West Country accent

explanation.surface: Informal clothes for someone eating in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a pun: in a Devon accent 'sweet eater' runs together into the knitwear word.
explanation.definitionFit: A jumper is pulled on for informal dress; a sweet-eater blurred in West Country speech gives the same sound.
